item.title: Takeoff Estate Seeks Dismissal
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Takeoff's estate requested dismissal of the longstanding sexual assault lawsuit, citing allegedly deleted text message evidence.
item.content:encoded:
Takeoff‘s mother, Titiana Davenport, and estate sought dismissal of his rape accuser’s lawsuit over alleged text deletions after she sued, MyNewsLA reported. Their October 27 motion cited her October 14 deposition.

The woman, identified in court as Jane Doe, sued the Migos rapper in Los Angeles Superior Court on August 5, 2020. Her complaint accused him of sexual battery, assault, false imprisonment and inflicting emotional distress. The allegations concerned an Encino house party.

According to the complaint obtained by Rolling Stone, Doe had been in touch with DJ Durel, whose real name is Daryl McPherson, through social media before going to the party to meet him. She alleged that Takeoff’s repeated advances at the party had made her feel uncomfortable. The suit also alleged gender violence and civil rights violations.

Doe said she told Durel she did not want an intimate relationship with Takeoff. After an argument between the two men, she went to Durel’s bedroom. She alleged that Takeoff entered, ignored her refusal to have sex and raped her. The complaint placed the alleged assault at 2 a.m. on June 23. It also said she sought care at a hospital, where staff saw evidence of rape and notified police.

Her attorney, Neama Rahmani, told SPIN in 2020 that he normally would have waited for a criminal investigation to end before suing. He said more than a month had passed without an arrest or charges and hoped the lawsuit would bring forward witnesses and evidence. LAPD confirmed an active investigation to SPIN.

Takeoff denied the allegations through attorney Drew Findling, who told SPIN his team had reviewed them. Findling said: “What has become abundantly clear is that the allegations made against Takeoff are patently and provably false.”

In April 2021, the Los Angeles County district attorney’s office declined to prosecute because of insufficient evidence, a spokesperson confirmed to Pitchfork. Rahmani criticized that decision in a statement to the outlet and said Doe remained committed to her civil case. “She looks forward to receiving the justice she deserves in her civil case,” he said.

Takeoff was shot and killed in Houston on November 1, 2022. He was 28.

A hearing is set for January 21, 2027.

item.title: Hoolibaby Neeno Taps Into Southern Street Culture With New Single “Nike Box”
item.dc:creator: Brxton Lee
item.description: Louisiana rapper Hoolibaby Neeno turns the Nike box into a symbol of the hustle on his new single "Nike Box," out today.
item.content:encoded:
The Plain Dealing, Louisiana rapper explores the cultural significance of sneaker culture, street entrepreneurship, and the hustle that shaped a generation.

Rising Louisiana rapper Hoolibaby Neeno continues to carve out his place in Southern hip-hop with the release of his new single, “Nike Box,” out today. Inspired by the deeper meaning behind a familiar symbol of street culture, the record explores the connection between sneaker culture, money, status, and the everyday hustle that has shaped generations of young people.

For many growing up in the hood, Nikes represented more than sneakers; they symbolized respect, pride, and the feeling of making it with limited resources. The Nike box itself became part of that culture, often repurposed to hold hard-earned cash. Through “Nike Box,” Neeno draws on this shared experience to tell a story rooted in resourcefulness, street entrepreneurship, and the realities of growing up with little.

Reflecting on the record’s inspiration, Neeno explains, “For an urban kid coming up in the hood, Nikes were more than just sneakers; they represented status, respect, pride, and the feeling of making it when you had very little. The Nike box itself became just as valuable as the shoes inside, serving as a symbol of the culture and the hustle that shaped an entire generation.”

Hailing from Plain Dealing, Louisiana, Neeno represents a new generation of Southern artists influenced by the region’s rich hip-hop legacy. Drawing inspiration from the Hot Boys, Trill Entertainment, Webbie, Boosie, Lil Phat, and Kevin Gates, he blends raw street storytelling with melodic hooks and an unmistakable Southern perspective. Neeno continues to build his catalog through records such as “Sweet Lady,” “24,” “Clap Clap,” and “Bend Ya Back,” alongside projects including Squeeki Son and Paid In Full.

His growing momentum is reflected in his streaming presence, alongside expanding his visibility through his “Sweet Lady” performance on On The Radar, adding to his growing footprint as an independent artist. With “Nike Box,” Neeno continues to bring the experiences and influences that shaped him to the forefront, building on Louisiana’s rich hip-hop legacy while carving out his own lane in Southern rap. Stay tuned for more music and visuals from Hoolibaby Neeno coming soon.

About Hoolibaby Neeno

Hoolibaby Neeno is a rising independent rapper from Plain Dealing, Louisiana, bringing the raw energy and Southern soul of the 318 to a new generation of hip-hop. Influenced by the Hot Boys, Trill Entertainment, Webbie, Boosie, Lil Phat, and Kevin Gates, Neeno combines street-rooted storytelling with melodic hooks. Through releases including “Sweet Lady,” “24,” “Clap Clap,” and “Bend Ya Back,” as well as projects Squeeki Son and Paid In Full, he continues to establish his identity as an emerging voice in Southern rap while remaining connected to the culture and community that shaped him.

item.title: I Might’ve Just Found Hip-Hop’s Most Underrated Group in 2026.
item.dc:creator: Staff Writer
item.description: Rooted In Power may be a new name to you, but Joshua Dunn and MrGrippz bring 15 years of chemistry to their self-produced debut, Side By Side.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years is a long time to keep creating with somebody.

Long enough for the initial excitement to wear off. Long enough for “we should make something together” to either become real work or one of those conversations nobody brings up anymore.

That’s the detail that caught my attention about Rooted In Power. Joshua Dunn, from Tiffin, Ohio, and MrGrippz, from Hollywood, Florida, spent 15 years collaborating across state lines before fully committing to the duo and the name they now share. These aren’t two strangers putting together a project and hoping chemistry shows up. There’s history here. Rooted In Power Media Info

Their debut album, Side By Side, arrives with that history behind it. The surprise release brings together 14 tracks, accompanied by a video for the title song. A new name for some listeners, sure. But hardly a first attempt at making something together. musicwire.popfiltr.com

And that distinction is worth paying attention to.

A Debut Doesn’t Always Mean Beginners

The part of Rooted In Power’s story I keep coming back to is how much responsibility these two have taken for the music.

Dunn and MrGrippz wrote, produced and arranged the entire album themselves. Both are emcees and producers, making this a partnership that extends beyond trading verses. They’re responsible for what gets said, what sits underneath it and how the songs come together. Rooted In Power Media Info

There’s something appealing about that level of involvement. Not because outside collaborators are a problem. Great records get made that way every day. But when two people handle the writing, production and arrangements, those credits give you a very clear place to look for the identity of the project.

The decisions belong to them.

For a listener discovering Rooted In Power, that’s a useful introduction. You’re getting a body of work shaped by the same two people whose names are on the front. There’s room to get acquainted, rather than trying to figure out who an artist is from one isolated single.

“Side By Side” Takes Commitment Seriously

The title track offers an especially human way into their world.

The duo describes “Side By Side” as a rough-edged love song about the push and pull of a romantic relationship. Co-produced by Dunn and MrGrippz, it centers loyalty and passion without pretending that staying together comes without struggles. Rooted In Power Media Info

That’s a subject with some life in it.

Falling for somebody is one story. Figuring out how to keep choosing each other is another. The second one has less room for fantasy and a lot more room for pride, patience and uncomfortable conversations.

A love song doesn’t have to ignore those things to be romantic. Sometimes acknowledging the difficult parts makes the commitment mean more.

That’s also what makes Side By Side such a fitting title for this introduction to Rooted In Power. The song concerns a romantic relationship, but there’s an interesting parallel in the group’s own history: two people continuing to make things together over a substantial stretch of their lives.

Different kinds of relationships, obviously. Still, the connection gives the title another layer. Commitment isn’t an abstract idea in their story. Their working relationship gives it a timeline.

There’s More To This Introduction

The title video is also the beginning of a larger visual rollout. Rooted In Power says additional videos have already been prepared, with each release intended to develop the album’s visual story further. Rooted In Power Media Info

So there’s somewhere to go after the first click.

For me, that’s the appeal of discovering an act like this. There’s a partnership to learn about, a full project to spend time with and a song built around something recognizable outside of music.

No elaborate explanation required. Two people. Years of work. A record with their fingerprints all over it.

“Underrated” is ultimately a judgment listeners get to make. Rooted In Power has given them something to judge.

Start with the “Side By Side” video. Then give the album some room.

The name might be new to you. The work behind it isn’t.

item.title: LoWick Killed At 22 In FBI Shooting
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: LoWick died at 22 after an FBI agent shot him during a federal operation in Dixmoor, as his family questioned the shooting.
item.content:encoded:
LoWick died at 22 after an FBI agent shot him in Dixmoor, Illinois, on October 28. The rapper’s real name was Chadwick Clark. His sister, Nia Cole, told the Chicago Sun-Times he had a 2-year-old daughter.

The shooting took place around 7 a.m. near 145th Street and Cooper Avenue. Village officials told WGN-TV that federal agents had come to serve a search warrant. The Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office said a 22-year-old man died about an hour after the shooting, Patch reported. The office placed the incident in the 14500 block of South Cooper Avenue.

Cole told ABC7 Chicago her brother was inside the home and had no weapon. She also said, “The warrant was for his arrest, not for the house.”

The FBI had not explained what led agents to open fire or disclosed the details of the warrant.

In her Sun-Times interview, Cole said her brother was trying to move past his troubles. He was the youngest of nine children and was due to start a job at Amazon. She said his rap lyrics did not reflect his life and the guns in his videos were props.

According to FOX 32 Chicago, LoWick had made songs and appeared in videos with Bloodhound Q50.

Bloodhound Q50 was buried in September, after he was killed at a gas station in Chicago’s Fuller Park neighborhood. Police from several Northwest Indiana agencies helped secure his funeral procession through Merrillville.

Nearby residents also described the morning gunfire to ABC7. Ruth Perkins said she heard roughly six shots and then someone call for an ambulance. The station later saw agents carry large white boxes out of the house.

Cole told the Sun-Times she last spoke with LoWick the night before he died. The next morning, his girlfriend told her he was dead. Cole was at Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn at the time. “All he talked about was getting off parole and taking care of his daughter,” she said. She had lost another brother to a fatal stabbing in 2013.

The FBI said none of its staff were hurt. Its Inspection Division was reviewing the shooting.

item.title: Prince’s 3121 Vault Opens
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Prince's estate previewed expanded 3121 with an unreleased song and a December release paired with a Vegas concert film.
item.content:encoded:
Prince‘s estate previewed an expanded 3121 with the unreleased “Time of Ur Life,” setting a December 11 release.

The 12-song album gains 10 bonus tracks, including acoustic versions of “The Word,” “Love” and “Te Amo Corazón.” Digital, two-CD/Blu-ray and three-LP/Blu-ray editions are planned, Variety reported.

“Prince: 3121 Las Vegas Concert” reaches U.S. and Canadian theaters December 3. Tickets go on sale November 11. The 154-minute film and Blu-ray capture his January 20, 2007, show.

The album marked a major chart return. 3121 became his fourth Billboard 200 No. 1, as AllHipHop previously reported. His last had been the Batman soundtrack in 1989, a gap of 17 years. Its first week brought 183,000 U.S. sales and a No. 1 debut on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, too.

His official channel has a “Lolita” clip from the concert.

That Vegas run put him in a much smaller setting than an arena. In a firsthand review of the residency, Travel Weekly writer Ellen Sterling described a converted showroom at the Rio, with most fans on their feet and limited tables along the walls.

At the show she attended, Prince performed from 12:30 a.m. until 2:30 a.m. He played “Black Sweat” and “Te Amo Corazón” alongside “Kiss,” but left out “When Doves Cry” despite requests. Sterling described a small stage with musicians on several levels and low lighting that made her listen more closely.

The original album mixed several styles. Pitchfork critic Joe Tangari heard Latin rhythms alongside electronic funk, pointing to the horns on “Get On the Boat” and synthesizers on “Love.”

The album also made its mark at the 2007 Grammys. The Recording Academy nominated 3121 for Best R&B Album, with its title track up for Best Urban/Alternative Performance. “Black Sweat” earned two nominations: Best R&B Song and Best Male R&B Vocal Performance.

Prince shared another nomination with singer Támar for “Beautiful, Loved and Blessed,” in the Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group With Vocals category.

3121 arrived in stores March 21, 2006. The 3121 Las Vegas Live concert album is due November 27 on vinyl and CD for Record Store Day Black Friday.

item.title: Kirk Franklin Says Kanye Offered Beats Without Taking Credit
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Kirk Franklin said Kanye West offered beats without credit to spare Christian listeners' feelings, but he refused the plan.
item.content:encoded:
Kirk Franklin said Kanye West once offered him beats with no public credit to avoid upsetting Christians. He refused to accept the music on those terms.

“Because that sends a message that your gift is good enough, but you’re not,” Franklin told Nessa on HOT 97.

He recalled West arriving at his home with his father and cousin the day after Thanksgiving in 2014. West had driven from Oklahoma, where he had relatives. Franklin said West and his dad ate all his Thanksgiving leftovers. West wanted to help the genre, Franklin said.

Franklin and West shared a public gospel moment in 2016. Franklin appeared on “Ultralight Beam,” the opener on West’s 2016 album The Life of Pablo. He also joined West on “Saturday Night Live,” a performance AllHipHop covered that brought gospel, rap and R&B artists to the same stage.

That question of who gets welcomed into gospel has followed Franklin for decades. In a 2016 PBS interview, he described criticism from traditional churchgoers over his sound and stage moves. The report traced how “Stomp” reached R&B and Hip-Hop charts and secular radio in 1997.

That reach had roots in his 1993 debut, Kirk Franklin and the Family, which spent 100 weeks on the gospel charts. Franklin told PBS that religious rules could get in the way of a person’s relationship with God. He saw falling church attendance among young people as part of the challenge.

Franklin’s latest music has kept those doors open. His September deal with Uptown Records brought him to the label Andre Harrell founded, with a history that includes Mary J. Blige, Jodeci and Heavy D & The Boyz.

Ahead of I Am What I Am, Franklin discussed the cost of crossing those lines in a separate interview with Audacy’s Big Mack. He said rejection from his own faith community could hurt more than the creative fight itself. The album’s title, he explained, reflected how much of his life he had spent trying to show his love for Jesus, even when listeners questioned him.

Apple Music listed the 14-song set for October 30, with GloRilla, Davido and Jelly Roll among its guests.

item.title: LL Cool J Books Vegas
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: LL Cool J set an 11-show Las Vegas residency for 2027, with presales opening this week and dates split between May and July.
item.content:encoded:
LL Cool J booked 11 Las Vegas shows for “Rock The Bells: The Residency” at Dolby Live at Park MGM in 2027.

The dates are May 15, 16, 19, 21 and 22, plus July 9, 10, 11, 14, 16 and 17.

All shows start at 8 p.m., with guest performances and storytelling planned.

“Hip-Hop started in a few neighborhoods in New York, and now it belongs to the whole world. Along the way it changed rock, R&B, pop, soul, dance music, all of it. Rock The Bells celebrates everybody who was part of that story,” LL Cool J said.

The run comes as LL has been talking about what makes fans stay with an artist. In a “7PM in Brooklyn” interview released October 16, he urged rappers to put songs ahead of clicks.

His point was about the ties music can build, even when the numbers take time to catch up.

He spoke about the pain of putting care into a song and seeing it draw little interest. The answer, he said, was to keep making music and let a core audience grow.

He also used basketball to explain why stats could fall short. A player’s value to teammates might never show up in a box score.

For artists, chasing a quick response could leave the feeling in a song behind.

That focus had shaped his own return to recording. In a July 2024 interview with The Associated Press, LL described the work behind The FORCE, his first album in 11 years.

He had spent time in the studio during that gap, then began to push harder. At first, he felt the beats he received were stronger than the verses he wrote. Q-Tip became his partner on the project and produced every track.

The process pushed LL to rethink his craft rather than coast on what had worked before. “I wasn’t trying to do trendy, and I wasn’t trying to recapture anything I did before,” he told AP.

He compared that work to great basketball players returning to practice to improve. His aim was to share where he stood as an artist and leave listeners free to take their own meaning from it.

Citi/AAdvantage presales start October 30 at 10 a.m. PT; MGM Rewards, Live Nation and Ticketmaster follow October 31, same time. General sales begin November 2 at 10 a.m. PT.

item.title: Cordae May Have Announced A Baby, But He Forgot One Detail
item.dc:creator: illseed
item.description: Cordae’s “Helpless” lyric hints at a second child, leaving BIG questions about the mother.
item.content:encoded:
Hold on, Cordae.

Bro slipped a possible baby announcement into “Helpless,” then left out the detail everybody wants: Who is the mother?

I love that song and I hit the rewind button a few times. On his joint album with Anderson .Paak, Heavy Is the Crown the rapper delivers a line that sounds like a major life change:

“I’m finna have my second child, although we still ain’t said our vows.”

Cordae does not identify the mother or provide a due date in the song. So, now we have nothing except speculation.

Naturally, Naomi Osaka’s name enters the conversation. She and Cordae share daughter Shai, born in July 2023, and Osaka publicly confirmed their breakup in January 2025. As AllHipHop previously reported, “Helpless” also finds Cordae reflecting on the disappointment of raising their daughter in separate homes. That sucks. It also gives the song an emotional connection to their past, but in no way establishes that Osaka is expecting another child with him.

Could the lyric refer to another relationship Cordae has kept private? Possibly. Probably. Could listeners be missing context about when the verse was written? Also possible. It might just be a bar, right?

Then there is the idea that he may be considering marriage, I marriage something he is contemplating or using to describe his circumstances? The rhyme opens the door to the rumor.

Still, Cordae certainly knows how to leave fans curious. We have had plenty of surprise announcements through music, and this sounds like a significant one.

If congratulations are in order, wonderful!

Til then, listen to the album.

item.title: Drake’s Next Move Could Make His Last $400 Million Deal Look Small
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: DJ Akademiks claims Drake could be approaching the largest recording contract in music history.
item.content:encoded:
Drake may be preparing to make music industry history with a record deal so enormous that his next album could be the least interesting part of the conversation. And they say nobody is making money in music anymore.

And then there is the source material.

DJ Akademiks has been talking about the Toronto superstar’s next business move. We’ll take it with a grain of salt for now.  The suggestion is that Drake could be approaching the biggest recording agreement in music history. Yes, bigger than the reported $400 million arrangement he previously secured with Universal Music Group.

Now, before anybody starts counting somebody else’s millions, we need to establish this is speculation. And we also do not yet know what company might be preparing to write this extraordinary check. In the past, it has been sad that Universal might be willing to do it despite their issues.

But Akademiks has historically had access to Drake’s business and therefore we have to take this serious.

During an appearance on “One Night with Steiny,” Akademiks said Drake has satisfied his previous contractual obligations and could be positioning himself for another monumental payday.

We all know Drake’s relationship with Universal Music Group has been complicated by his legal dispute involving Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.” That controversy raised questions about the relationship between one of the industry’s most commercially successful rappers and the corporation responsible for distributing his music. We also know money is all folks care about and nothing is personal.

So, would Drake return to Universal for another colossal arrangement? Would a competing company be able to pony official money to woo him? Or could he negotiate something that gives him substantially more ownership and control?

Money, ownership and control seem the same but very different.

A deal exceeding $400 million would certainly command attention, but the structure matters. An advance against future royalties is not the same as receiving hundreds of millions outright. Catalog rights, distribution arrangements and recording commitments could all influence the final valuation.

Never forget Drake is one of the few rappers whose commercial reach makes this even a rumor.

Stay tuned.

Neither Drake nor UMG has publicly confirmed the rumored contract so we’ll be watching til something materializes.

He’s probably looking at these reports like:

item.title: Ali Shaheed Muhammad Leaves A Tribe Called Quest Reunion Door Open
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Ali Shaheed Muhammad left room for a Tribe Called Quest reunion while explaining the grief of performing without Phife Dawg.
item.content:encoded:
Ali Shaheed Muhammad left the possibility of an A Tribe Called Quest reunion open while explaining why performing without Phife Dawg remained difficult.

In his interview about Tribe’s future, Muhammad told Clash that the group still struggled with the loss of a member whose presence shaped its shows.

“We haven’t figured it out yet,” Muhammad said when discussing how Tribe might move forward without Phife beside them.

He also left room for another chapter: “I can’t answer, but I’m always open to the possibility of something.”

Muhammad described the connection between Q-Tip and Phife onstage as something the remaining members could not simply replace with another performance.

He explained that Tribe had not prepared for that absence, contrasting their experience with De La Soul continuing to perform during Dave’s illness.

He recalled understanding the Beastie Boys’ reluctance to perform after MCA’s death much better once he experienced losing Phife himself.

Phife died in March 2016, and Tribe subsequently marked another ending during its appearance at New York City’s Panorama festival in July 2017.

Q-Tip, Muhammad and Jarobi White told the hometown crowd that the performance would be their last New York show as A Tribe Called Quest.

Meanwhile, Muhammad’s partnership with Adrian Younge continued with The Midnight Hour: Lost Tapes JID028, which arrived through Jazz Is Dead on October 23.

The nine-track album grew from sessions for a second Midnight Hour project that were set aside in 2020 as Jazz Is Dead took priority.

Their first Midnight Hour album arrived in 2018, drawing on a live rhythm section and an orchestra for recordings made directly to tape.

Muhammad also worked with Raphael Saadiq and Dawn Robinson in Lucy Pearl, adding another group to a career spanning rap and R&B.

Muhammad and Younge also reached television through Marvel’s Luke Cage, bringing their music to the Netflix superhero series set in Harlem.

Their production appeared on Kendrick Lamar’s untitled unmastered., including “untitled 06,” which featured CeeLo Green and began as music for their own project.

On the new album, Muhammad played electric bass and drums on “The Midnight Stroll,” while Younge handled acoustic piano, according to the official credits.
